items.title: National and International News in Focus: Nov. 12 | National | wktv.com
items.excerpt: ## Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after his affair raises national security concerns Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is resigning after his affair raises national security concerns. The company named Colette Kress as interim CEO on Thursday. She is the current executive vice president and chief financial officer. Huang faced growing calls to resign after his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Late Wednesday, media reports said Huang had another extramarital affair with an Nvidia employee who reported to him. Shares of Nvidia, one of the largest companies in the world, plunged 10% in premarket trading Thursday. ## 5 people are shot in a trendy DC neighborhood, including 1 killed at a gym, a witness says WASHINGTON (AP) — Authorities say five people have been shot in a trendy Washington, D.C., neighborhood within walking distance of the White House. A witness says at least one of those shot was at a gym and died. Police say a shooting suspect was barricaded Thursday near the initial shooting site. The shootings were reported in Logan Circle, a mile north of the White House. The area includes a VIDA fitness center, St. Luke’s Episcopal Church, residences and a Whole Foods supermarket. Witness James Spellman was at the gym when he heard shots fired. Spellman says a man was shot in the neck, fell to the ground and died in a pool of blood. ## US envoys meet with Putin in Moscow on Ukraine talks, then head for Dublin to see Zelenskyy MOSCOW (AP) — U.S. envoys held talks about the fighting in Ukraine with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin. The meeting, which lasted about two hours on Thursday, follows U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi. The talks resulted in an agreement on a large prisoner exchange, though no breakthrough was made in ending the nearly 5-year-old conflict. The U.S. envoys aim to involve Europe in negotiations, but Moscow is resistant. They will now head to Dublin, Ireland, to brief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He sees a political opportunity for peace due to changes in the U.S. Congress and upcoming elections in Europe. Meanwhile, fighting continues, and Ukraine faces new disruptions in its Starlink internet service. ... ## Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills 6 people, including a doctor and a child, Health Ministry says KHAN YOUNIS, Gaza Strip (AP) — Gaza’s Health Ministry says an Israeli airstrike has hit one of the main hospitals still operating in the Gaza Strip, killing six people, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy. The Israeli military said the strike Thursday on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza was targeting a Hamas commander and other militants, without providing evidence. The commander it identified was not among the dead. The ministry and witnesses said the strike hit the hospital’s surgical wing. Footage showed several wards and operating rooms heavily damaged or destroyed, with debris scattered across hospital beds and equipment and rebar dangling from holes in the ceiling. At least 28 people were wounded. ## Death toll rises to 8 in Brooklyn building collapse as rescuers dig through rubble NEW YORK (AP) — At least eight people have died after a three-story building in Brooklyn collapsed at the edge of a construction site. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the death toll Thursday morning as firefighters continued to dig through the rubble in the search for others. The building, adjacent to a construction site, collapsed on Wednesday afternoon. Rescuers worked overnight, using dogs to sniff for survivors. The cause of the collapse is under investigation. The three-story building was a mixed-use structure with apartments above commercial space. Mamdani says at least 17 people have been injured, including three firefighters.

items.title: Stubborn inflation raises prospect of more aggressive Federal Reserve rate hikes
items.excerpt: **Why it matters:** Fed officials had hoped that a relatively modest series of interest rate hikes would be enough to bring inflation under control — more a recalibration than a tightening campaign. * But stubbornly high — and increasingly widespread — price pressures are raising the possibility of a more prolonged tightening campaign, with no clear endpoint in sight. * That would leave the Fed facing a more difficult balancing act: raising rates enough to contain inflation without unnecessarily damaging the economy. ... **Driving the news:** Treasury yields are surging after Tuesday's hot inflation report and hawkish commentary from Fed officials — including governor Christopher Waller, who raised the prospect of a supersized rate hike next month. * Short-term yields have risen more sharply than longer-term yields, a sign that investors expect the Fed may need to raise rates more aggressively than previously anticipated. * The yield on the two-year Treasury note is still marching higher after surging 17 basis points on Tuesday, which was the biggest one-day surge since April 2025 — when markets were reeling from the "liberation day" tariffs. * The yield on the 10-year Treasury note jumped about 8 basis points, putting it back above 5%. * Financial markets see a December rate hike as virtually certain, according to CME FedWatch. Expectations for next year are trending higher, with traders now pricing in two additional quarter-point hikes by June. **The big picture: **Measures designed to strip out unusually large price swings suggest that underlying inflation pressures are gaining pace. * The Cleveland Fed's trimmed-mean Consumer Price Index —which filters out unusually large price swings to give a clearer picture of underlying inflation — rose 0.4% in October, the largest monthly increase since May. * The Atlanta Fed's sticky-price CPI, which tracks prices that typically change, slowly accelerated to a 4.7% annualized pace in October, its fastest since February 2025. * More than three-quarters of the consumer price basket saw prices rise at an annualized rate exceeding 2% in October, the largest share since August 2022, Charles Schwab's head of macro research Kevin Gordon posted on X. **Yes, but: **The Fed may have reason to proceed cautiously even against the backdrop of stubborn inflation. * Rising bond yields and a sell-off in technology stocks (revived again by the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang) are already tightening financial conditions — potentially doing some of the work of higher interest rates. * Fed governor Michelle Bowman said in a speech that falling stock prices, higher borrowing costs and a stronger dollar could weigh on economic growth, particularly in sectors already struggling with high interest rates. * Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who dissented against the decision to hold rates steady last month, said she still supported a more gradual approach to raising rates. "It's less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements," she said Thursday morning.

items.title: As Higher Prices Seep into Broader Economy, Fed Officials Consider Faster Hikes | Industrial Distribution
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON (AP) — More evidence this week of hot inflation in the U.S. was unpleasant news for the Federal Reserve, not to mention consumers: Rising prices may be spreading beyond the one-time shocks from tariffs and high gas prices into the wider economy, meaning that mortgages, credit cards and other forms of borrowing are likely to become increasingly expensive. Tuesday's consumer price index report showed broadly rising costs across a range of goods and services, some with little connection to more expensive oil and gas or surging investment in artificial intelligence data centers, another factor blamed for worsening inflation. And there is increasing anxiety among Fed officials that higher oil prices stemming from the Iran war may last longer than previously thought. A key issue debated by Fed policymakers for months has been whether inflation would cool on its own if the Iran war ended and oil prices fell and as the impact of tariffs faded. But government data suggested inflation rose to 4% in October compared with a year ago, up from 3.7% in September, even as gas prices leveled off. The potential consequences of the new inflation data emerged immediately. Two Fed officials suggested Tuesday that the central bank may have to hike its key interest rate more quickly to tame inflation. Bigger or faster hikes by the Fed would mean that buying a house or a car, or paying off a credit card would become a steeper hill to climb, with millions of Americans already struggling to make ends meet. Lorie Logan, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas and a voting member of the Fed's rate-setting committee, said Tuesday that price increases remain high for services such as "visits to the doctor, childcare, dining out and hotel stays." "Prices for these services aren't particularly sensitive to tariffs, conflict in the Middle East or surging demand for computer chips," she added. "While I expect inflation to moderate as price pressures dissipate in energy and manufactured goods, the broader inflationary trend is more likely to persist." Logan said Tuesday she supported two additional quarter-point rate hikes. While she has made similar statements before, Logan added that the Fed could "move more rapidly this winter" than it "has moved so far this fall," signaling that she may support two rate hikes in a row, a quicker pace than the Fed's current approach. ... But surging investment in data centers has driven up the cost of computer chips, power generation equipment, and copper, among other components, with little sign of easing. Prices for smartphones jumped 1.4% just from September to October, the government said, the largest such increase on record.
